name: Kuliah 11_PHARMACODINAMICS
text:
PHARMACODYNAMIC
N U R L A I L I S U S A N T I
D I V I S I FA R M A KO L O G I
P S P D U I N M AU L A N A M A L I K I B R A H I M M A L A N G
PHARMACODYNAMIC
❑The action of a drug on the body to produce biological effect →
What drug does to the body
Factors affecting the effects of a drug
MECHANISM OF DRUG ACTION
• Important for determining the rational therapies and new 
drug design.
• Drug mechanisms can be classified into 4 types:
-
Drugs that work through no specific targets : antacids, general 
anesthesia, osmotic diuretic
-
Drugs that work by changing the transport system : calcium 
antagonists, cardiac glycosides, local anesthetic
-
Drugs that work by changing the enzyme function : COX 
Inhibitors, MAO Inhibitors, ACE Inhibitors
-
Drugs acting on receptors: Hormones, Neurotransmitters
DRUG TARGET
• The effect of a drug occurs when it binds to its specific 
molecule. The specific molecule is a binding site called a 
drug target.
• Four primary drug targets are:
a.
Receptors
b.
Ion channels
c.
Enzymes
d.
Transporter
• Most specific part that binds to the drug is a protein, 
except:
– Antitumour and antimicrobial drugs bind directly to DNA
– Biphosponat bind calcium salts on bone matrix
– Heavy metal bind to small molecules metalloproteinases
A. ION CHANNELS
• Ion channels are protein molecules that span the cell membrane, and 
can switch between open and closes states, allowing the controlled 
entry or exit of specific ions across the cell membrane. 
• Drugs may bind within the ion channel and prevent the flow of ions 
or may bind elsewhere on the molecule and increase or decrease the 
probability of the channel opening.
• Ex. Local anaesthetics, which block pain pathways by blocking sodium 
channels and therefore preventing the action potential that carries the 
pain signal from the site of injury to the brain
B. ENZYME
• Drugs can mimics the natural substrate acting as a competitive 
inhibitor of the enzyme, (ex: captopril/ ACE inhibitor), or non-competitive 
inhibitor (ex: aspirin/ COX inhibitor)
• Drugs may also act as false substrates, where the drug molecule 
undergoes transformation to form an abnormal product that subverts 
the normal metabolic pathway.  Ex. anticancer drug, fluorouracil, replaces 
uracil, so cannot be converted into thymidylate → block DNA synthesis 
and prevent cell division. 
• Prodrug is activated by enzymes to become active drug
C. TRANSPORTER/ CARRIER MOLECULES
• Transportation of polar molecules across lipid membranes often 
requires a carrier protein. The carrier proteins embody a recognition 
site that makes them specific for a particular permeating species, and 
these sites can also be targets for drugs, whose effect is generally to 
block the transporter. 
• Ex. Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) for depression.
D. RECEPTORS
• The macromolecular component of the cell which specifically 
recognise a drug molecule and upon binding undergo a conformation 
change leading to activation/ inhibition of cell signalling.
• Receptors are generally Proteins
• Molecules that can act as a receptor:
– Enzyme (class of tyrosine kinase)
– Membrane protein (Glycoprotein, Lipoprotein)
– Nucleic acid (Antibiotic receptors)
– Polysaccharide complex
Receptor characteristics
• has specificity "lock and key mechanism"
• produce a selective response
• has sensitivity
TYPE OF PROTEIN AT THE RECEPTOR
• Transport: mediates ion ex. transport Na/K ATPase in 
digitalis glycosides
• Regulator: mediates the action of endogenous ligand, ex. 
hormone
• Enzyme: inhibits/ activates, ex. Dihidrofolase reductase
• Structural/ Anchor: integrated in cell structure, ex. tubulin 
(colchicine receptor)
TYPES OF RECEPTOR
1. LIGAND GATED ION CHANNELS
• Ionotropic receptor
• Receptor bind to an ion channel.  The 
ligand binding to this receptor causes 
the opening of the ion channel so that 
it will convert the membrane 
potential into depolarization or 
hyperpolarization depending on the 
incoming / outgoing ions. 
• Usually receptor for the 
neurotransmitters → mediate fast 
signal transmission at synapses
• Ex. Receptors acethilcholine nicotinic 
(nAChR), Glutamat (NMDA)
2. G-PROTEIN COUPLED RECEPTORS (GPCR)
• Metabotropic receptor
• transmembrane protein composed of several subunits (αβγ), sub 
unit α has GTPase activity (inhibitory or stimulatory).
• The most common receptor 
• Ex: receptor for biogenic amines, eicosanoids, fat signaling molecule, 
peptide, protein ligands
• The ligand will bind to the binding site in the extracellular part, 
then activate G protein by converting GDP to GTP which forms a 
complex with the receptor. The active G protein will activate target 
protein and provide cellular effects
• Target for GPCR:
– Adenilat siklase
– Phospolipase C
– Ion Channel (esp. Ca2+ and K+)
– Rho A kinase
– MAP Kinase
GPCR desensitization
GPCRs can undergo phosphorylation 
that interferes coupling between G 
proteins with effector proteins
•
Fosforilation
The phosphorylation in PKA and PKC 
produce not specific effect so it can 
affect other receptors → 
heterologous desensitization
•
Internalization
The phosphorylation in GRK (GPC 
Receptor Kinase) are very specific 
and act as binding sites of beta 
arrestin (intracellular proteins that 
block G protein interactions)
→ homologous desensitization
3. KINASE-LINKED RECEPTORS
• Large transmembrane protein with a large 
amount of residue. 
• The molecules involved in the signaling 
pathway after the drug binds to the 
receptor are called second messengers
• The receptor controls growth and 
differentiation and regulates gene 
transcription. 
• 3 types of receptor kinase :
o Tyrosine kinase receptor: epidermal 
growth factor, nerve growth factor, toll-
like receptor
o Serine/ Treonin kinase receptor : 
transforming growth factor
o The cytokine receptor: has no 
intrinsic enzyme activity, if it is activated 
it will associate and activate another 
tyrosine kinase
4. NUCLEAR RECEPTORS
• Soluble proteins that bind to DNA 
and regulate the transcription of 
specific genes.
• grouped into 2:
– Type I: Receptors located in 
the cytoplasm in the form of 
dimer and translocated to the 
nucleus.  The ligand is generally 
the endocrine (steroid). Ex: 
Estrogen Receptor (ER)
– Type II: Receptors are in 
nucleus, heterodimer with 
Retinoid X receptor (RXR)   The 
ligand is generally lipid (fatty 
acid). Ex: PPAR
TYPES OF BINDING FORCES
• Drug receptor complex formation is promoted by chemical bonds 
between functional groups on the drug and the receptor.
• The strength of receptor binding depends on the type of bonds 
formed.
DRUG-RECEPTOR INTERACTIONS
• Agonist : Drugs interact with 
receptors and possess effect as 
natural ligand
• Antagonist : Drugs interact with 
receptors and block binding 
receptor with natural ligand
AGONIST
• Full Agonist: maximal efficacy
• Partial Agonist: less than 
maximal efficacy
Potency and Efficacy
• Potency is the amount of drug 
needed to produce the desired 
effect
• Efficacy is effects produced by a 
drug that depends on the number 
of doses
ANTAGONIST
• Competitive : bind reversibly to the same receptor site as the agonist 
→ the inhibitory effect can be reversed by adding more agonist.
• Non Competitive : bind irreversibly (covalent bond) or bind to a 
different site
CHANGE IN DRUG RESPONSE
• A drug may undergo a change in response 
from a supposed response at the same dose. 
– Tolerance : drug response decrease
– Sensitization : drug response increase
• Caused by 2 factors :
▪Innate : genetic → has been found since the 
drug was first given
▪Acquired :
- Pharmacokinetics, ex. changed speed of 
drug metabolism
- Pharmacodynamic, ex. changes in drug 
target
TOLERANCE
• A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic back pain had been 
taking oral morphine for three months. Initially, a 10 mg dose 
significantly reduced his pain. However, after several weeks, the 
patient reported no further relief from the same dose, so the doctor 
increased the dose to 20 mg.
Mechanism: down-regulation of opioid receptors, changes in 
intracellular signaling systems, or increased drug metabolism.
Clinical implications: Patients require higher doses to achieve 
the same effect, increasing the risk of side effects and addiction.
SENSITIZATION
• A 22-year-old woman with schizophrenia was receiving haloperidol 
(an antipsychotic). After 2 months of therapy, she began exhibiting 
symptoms of involuntary facial movements (grimaces, tongue 
thrusting) that worsened despite the dosage not being increased.
Mechanism: Mechanism: Up-regulation of dopamine D2 receptors 
to compensate for chronic inhibition by haloperidol.
Clinical implications: The emergence of side effects such as 
tardive dyskinesia, even when the dose remains constant or even 
decreased.
DOSE-RESPONSE RELATIONSHIP
• The relationship between the dose of a drug administered and the 
biological response or effect it produces 
• Interpretation of Dose-Response Curves:
• Potency (EC50): dose that produces 50% of the maximum effect.
• Efficacy (Emax): maximum response that the drug can achieve.
Standar dose-response curve
X-axis = drug dose (usually log dose to 
create a sigmoid curve).
Y-axis = response (% maximal effect).
Curve types:
• Graded responses : a continuous increase in effect with increasing 
dose, in individual → sigmoid curve → Emax, EC50
   Ex. lowering blood pressure by an antihypertensive
• Quantal Dose responses (all/ none responses): a certain response 
or absolutely no response, in a population → Sigmoid and Bell-
shaped curve → ED50, TD50, LD50
   Ex. seizure or not
Key Parameters in Quantal Dose–Response Curve:
• ED₅₀ (Effective Dose 50%): The dose that produces a therapeutic effect in 
50% of the population → Potency
• TD₅₀ (Toxic Dose 50%): The dose that produces a toxic effect in 50% of the 
population.
• LD₅₀ (Lethal Dose 50%): The dose that causes death in 50% of the test 
population (usually animals).
THERAPEUTIC WINDOW
• The smallest dose limit that provides a 
therapeutic effect (MEC: Minimum Effective 
Concentration) to the largest dose that does 
not cause toxicity (MTC: Minimum Toxic 
Concentration).
THERAPEUTIC INDEX (TI)
• The comparison between the toxic/lethal dose 
and the effective dose of a drug → to assess 
the relative safety of a drug in a population.
• TI = LD₅₀/ED₅₀ or TD₅₀/ED₅₀
• Small (narrow) TI → narrow safety range → 
high-risk drug, requiring close monitoring.
Ex: Digoxin, Warfarin
• Large (wide) TI → wide safety range → 
relatively safe drug.
Ex: Penicillin, Diazepam
DRUG INTERACTION
: modification of a drug response due to interaction with other components
Factors that play a role in drug interactions:
• Polypharmacy
• Patients are treated by several doctors
• Self medication
• Lack of patient understanding
Target of Drug Interaction
–
Drug-drug Interactions
Ex. Paracetamol + Codein → increased analgetic effect
–
Drug-food Interactions
Ex. Captopril (ACE inhibitor) + food → decrease the absorption of 
the drug
–
Drug-herb Interactions
Ex. Warfarin (Anticoagulant) + onions → increase the potential for 
bleeding in patients because inhibition of thromboxane synthesis
Stages of Drug Interaction
– Pharmaceutical stage: the drug interacts during the 
production stage by the manufacture
– Pharmacokinetic stage:  Absorbsi, Distribution, Metabolism 
and Excretion
– Pharmacodinamyc stage: drug target
Pharmacokinetic Stages Of Drug 
Interaction
– Absorpsion
• Changes in GI Ph
• Form complexes with other medications that are not absorbed
• Changes in GI motility
• Malabsorption
– Distribution
• Interaction with protein bonds
• Induction or inhibition of transport proteins
– Metabolism
• Induction or inhibition of enzyme
– Excretion
• Change in urine Ph
• Changes in active secretion of the renal tubules
• Changes in renal blood flow
Pharmacodinamics stages of drug 
interaction
• Addictive Effect, if the response of the drugs follows the sum formula
• Synergistic Effect, if the response from these drugs is greater but not 
the same as the effect of the addition
• Antagonistic Effect, If the drug response is opposite
Characteristics of drug that potential 
to cause interactions
• Drug with a narrow therapeutic window
• Drugs that affect changes in the body's physiological functions, ex. 
Antihypertension
• Drugs that have strong protein bonds, ex. Aspirin
• Drug that is metabolized through saturation kinetics, ex. Phenytoin
ADVERSE DRUG REACTION
• Adverse drug reaction (ADR): Response to drugs used in normal doses 
that are unexpected
• Drug-specific, Occurs at normal doses, not due to overdose or misuse
• Ex: penicillin → anaphylaxis, antalgin → urticaria
• Adverse drug event (ADE) : any unexpected medical events that arise 
during use of a drug, but is not necessarily caused by the drug
• Not always a direct causal relationship to the drug.
• Include: Medication errors, drug poisoning due to overdose.
• Ex. : Patient fall due to dizziness after taking antihypertensive 
medication
Classification of ADR according to 
severity
• Mild: Does not affect patient’s daily activity
Ex. Urticaria after taking antalgin
• Moderate: Affects patient’s daily activity to some extent
Ex. Postural hypotension after taking antihypertension
• Severe: Affects patient's health may lead to death
Ex. Anafilactic shock after taking penicillin
Classification ADR according to 
immunological involvement → drug alergy
Type of drug side effect
Risk factors for adverse drug reaction
• Age (neonates, elderly)
• Gender (women > man) 
• Allergic disease (increased risk of reaction)
• Genetic factors (ex. Polymorphism in drug metabolism)
• Routes of administration (systemic > local)
TOPIK DISKUSI
Grafik berikut menunjukkan kurva log dosis-respon 4 
kandidat obat antihipertensi baru. Bagaimana perbandingan 
efikasi dan potensi ke-4 obat tersebut?
A
B
50%
Seorang pasien datang dengan riwayat asma dan sering 
menggunakan inhaler Salbutamol (agonis β-2 selektif) 
beberapa bulan terakhir. Awalnya pasien hanya menggunakan 
1 semprot untuk mengurangi gejala sesaknya, akan tetapi saat 
ini pasien harus menggunakan 2-3 semprot baru sesaknya 
menghilang. Jelaskan mengapa hal ini terjadi?
Obat A memiliki ED₅₀ = 2 mg/kg dan LD₅₀ = 200 mg/kg
Obat B memiliki ED₅₀ = 0,25 mg dan TD₅₀ = 0,5 mg
Hitunglah indeks terapi kedua obat tersebut dan interpretasikan makna 
klinisnya?
Tentukan kasus berikut termasuk ADR atau ADE
a.
Seorang pasien 25 tahun mendapat terapi penisilin untuk faringitis 
bakterial. Pada hari kedua, pasien mengalami gejala sesak, gatal, dan 
penurunan tekanan darah. Dokter mendiagnosis sebagai reaksi 
anafilaksis.
b.
Seorang pasien 15 tahun diberikan antalgin sesuai dosis. Setelah 
beberapa menit, muncul urtikaria gatal di seluruh tubuh.
c.
Seorang pasien 50 tahun dengan hipertensi baru mendapat terapi 
amlodipin. Pada minggu pertama, pasien mengeluh pusing dan 
terjatuh di kamar mandi sehingga mengalami fraktur.
d.
Seorang pasien kanker mendapat kemoterapi dengan doksorubisin 
dosis sesuai protokol. Setelah 4 siklus, pasien mengalami gagal 
jantung kongestif
e.
Seorang pasien 75 tahun dengan diabetes diberikan insulin. Perawat 
salah menghitung dosis, sehingga pasien menerima dua kali lipat 
dosis seharusnya dan kemudian mengalami hipoglikemia berat.
